Some of your team's most valuable business development work never appears in the headline numbers.

Someone builds a relationship, someone makes an introduction, and another person helps turn an opportunity into business. A pipeline total rarely captures all that effort.

My Business Development Performance Power BI Kit includes a dedicated view of team contributions and goals: https://garrettsdevdesk.etsy.com/listing/4595453904/power-bi-business-development-dashboard

The person who closes a deal isn't always the only person who helped create it.

An introduction might open the door, a referral might establish trust, and several colleagues may contribute expertise along the way. Those contributions can be easy to overlook when reporting focuses on opportunity ownership.

Try reviewing your last five won opportunities. Identify who led each one, who referred it, and who made meaningful supporting contributions.

It's difficult to recognize contributions that your reporting doesn't make visible.

Pipeline totals and opportunity ownership matter, but they may leave out referrals and supporting work that helped move business forward. A broader view can support more thoughtful conversations about team performance.

My Business Development Performance Power BI Kit includes lead, referral, and contributor reporting: https://garrettsdevdesk.etsy.com/listing/4595453904/power-bi-business-development-dashboard

Business development participation can look very different from person to person.

Some team members lead opportunities, others generate referrals, and others contribute specialized knowledge. Looking at those roles separately helps reveal involvement that a single activity total might hide.

Try building a simple contribution summary with three categories: lead, referral, and contributor. Compare participation across the team without treating overlapping credits as separate revenue.

Good business development reporting can help make more of the team's work visible.

Comparing opportunity leadership, referrals, contributor activity, and progress toward goals creates room for better conversations about recognition and development. It also helps explain how people support shared results.

A successful business development opportunity often has more people behind it than the final report suggests.

Relationships, referrals, introductions, and specialized contributions can all help move an opportunity forward. Making that work visible can support fairer recognition and more meaningful performance conversations.

For business development teams, what's one valuable contribution that tends to go unnoticed in your reporting?
